solution.concept_anchor: Unstarred questions — written answers, no supplementaries
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students associate 'placed on record' with being read aloud, conflating the procedural act of recording with oral delivery.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Oral answers are a feature of Starred questions, not Unstarred — Unstarred questions receive only written answers.
Eliminate option (c): Unstarred answers are placed in Lok Sabha records but are NOT read aloud in the House — the act of recording and oral reading are distinct.
Eliminate option (d): Supplementary questions are exclusively a feature of Starred questions; no supplementaries arise after Unstarred answers.
Confirm option (b): Unstarred questions receive only written answers, are placed on the record without being read out, and permit no supplementaries — (b) correctly states this.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here exploits the confusion between 'placed in records' and 'read out in the House.' A partially prepared student knows that Unstarred answers go on record and may wrongly conclude they are also read aloud — mirroring how ministerial statements are sometimes read. The correct understanding is that the written answer is simply appended to the proceedings without any oral delivery. This distinction also overlaps superficially with Zero Hour, making it a high-frequency confusion zone.
solution.final_explanation:
Starred and Unstarred questions are the two principal categories in Question Hour. A Starred question (marked with an asterisk) is intended for oral answer, and the oral delivery creates a live opportunity for the member to ask spontaneous follow-up — the supplementary question. An Unstarred question requires only a written answer, which is appended to the official proceedings of the House without being read aloud on the floor.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Oral answers are the defining feature of Starred, not Unstarred, questions.
• Option (b): Correct. Unstarred answers are given in writing, placed in the record without oral delivery, and no supplementaries are permitted.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Placement in the record is accurate but the claim of being 'read out' is false — this is the core trap.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Supplementary questions can only arise from a Starred question that has received an oral answer.

Value Addition:
• A member may submit up to one Starred and up to ten Unstarred questions per day.
• Only about 20 Starred questions are listed daily; the rest may be converted to Unstarred status through the ballot system.
• Supplementary questions must arise directly from the minister's oral answer — new subjects cannot be introduced.

solution.concept_anchor: Short Notice Questions vs. Zero Hour — prior notice distinction

statement_analysis.statement: A Short Notice Question is admitted on grounds of urgency and can be answered without the standard minimum notice period.
statement_analysis.reason: Short Notice Questions are exceptions to the 15-day notice rule; the Speaker/Chairman admits them when the matter is sufficiently urgent, allowing an oral answer without waiting for the standard period.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike Zero Hour, a Short Notice Question requires some form of prior notice to the Speaker/Chairman even if shorter than the prescribed minimum.
statement_analysis.reason: A Short Notice Question still requires a notice to be filed — it is the length, not the existence, of the notice that is reduced. Zero Hour, by contrast, requires no prior notice whatsoever.

statement_analysis.statement: The Minister is constitutionally bound to answer a Short Notice Question if the Speaker admits it.
statement_analysis.reason: A Minister retains the right to decline to answer a Short Notice Question if they are not prepared to do so — there is no constitutional compulsion to answer, only a procedural expectation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who correctly identify statements 1 and 2 but do not know the Minister's right to decline, leading them to include statement 3.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Short Notice Questions are admitted on urgency grounds with notice shorter than 15 days — this is a recognised procedural provision, so Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 2: A notice must still be given even for Short Notice Questions; Zero Hour alone operates without any notice — Statement 2 is correct.
Eliminate Statement 3: A Minister may decline to answer a Short Notice Question if unprepared — there is no constitutional or procedural compulsion to answer; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here merges two distinct concepts: the reduced notice of Short Notice Questions with the zero-notice feature of Zero Hour. Many students conflate these two devices as variations of the same thing. Additionally, statement 3 exploits the assumption that Speaker's admission of a question automatically compels a ministerial response — a plausible-sounding rule that does not exist in procedure.
solution.final_explanation:
Short Notice Questions and Zero Hour are frequently confused because both involve urgency and departures from standard procedure. However, they operate on fundamentally different bases. Short Notice Questions still require a formal notice — just shorter than the standard 15-day minimum — and the Speaker/Chairman decides admissibility based on the urgency of the matter. Zero Hour, starting at 12 noon, involves members raising issues entirely without prior notice.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Urgency is the admitted ground; the Speaker waives the standard notice period, not the requirement for notice itself.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The critical distinction from Zero Hour is that some notice must precede a Short Notice Question; Zero Hour has no such requirement at all.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: A Minister can decline to answer a Short Notice Question citing unpreparedness — admissibility by the Speaker does not remove this right.

Value Addition:
• Short Notice Questions, when admitted, are answered orally — making them similar in form but distinct in admission grounds from standard Starred questions.
• Zero Hour has no mention in the Constitution or Rules of Procedure — it is purely a parliamentary convention.
• The Speaker's decision on admissibility of questions is final; no appeal lies from this decision.

solution.concept_anchor: Notice period source — Rules of Procedure, not Constitution
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students naturally associate Parliament's fundamental procedures with the Constitution, not with subordinate procedural rules.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Lok Sabha (Speaker's Office) does not independently prescribe the notice period — it is governed by a formal rule, not a discretionary office practice.

Eliminate (b): The Constitution does not specify the notice period for questions; Article 118 grants Parliament the authority to make its own rules, but the specific period is fixed by those rules, not by the Constitution itself.
Eliminate (c): The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs administers parliamentary affairs but does not prescribe Question Hour notice periods.
Confirm (d): The 15-day notice requirement is prescribed by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha — the delegated procedural code under Article 118.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits students' tendency to attribute all fundamental parliamentary procedures to the Constitution. Article 118 empowers Parliament to make its own rules but does not specify notice periods. The actual 15-day minimum is set by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business — a delegated rule, not a constitutional provision. Students who answer 'the Constitution' conflate the enabling provision with the operative rule.
solution.final_explanation:
The 15-day minimum notice period for Starred and Unstarred questions is prescribed by the ________ and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha.

• Option (a): Incorrect — the Speaker's Office does not independently set procedural rules of this nature.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the Constitution (under Article 118) empowers Parliament to frame its own rules but does not itself prescribe notice periods.
• Option (c): Incorrect — the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs does not legislate procedural rules for Question Hour.
• Option (d): Correct — the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha is the operative document setting the 15-day requirement.

Value Addition:
• Article 118 authorises each House to make rules for regulating its own procedure — this is the constitutional basis for the Rules of Procedure.
• Short Notice Questions are the only exception to the 15-day rule, subject to Speaker's discretion.
• The Rules of Procedure are distinct from ordinary legislation — they do not require Presidential assent.

solution.concept_anchor: Questions addressable to private members — Lok Sabha Rule 40

statement_analysis.statement: Questions during Question Hour can only be addressed to ministers and never to private members of the House.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Lok Sabha Rule 40, a question can be addressed to a private member if it relates to a Bill, Resolution, or other matter for which that member is responsible — making the absolute claim 'never' false.

statement_analysis.statement: Questions during Question Hour are the exclusive prerogative of Opposition members; ruling party backbenchers cannot raise questions under this device.
statement_analysis.reason: Any member of the House — including ruling party backbenchers — is entitled to ask questions during Question Hour; questions are not restricted to the Opposition.

statement_analysis.statement: A question can be asked to a private member about a Bill introduced by that member in the House.
statement_analysis.reason: This is precisely the scenario envisaged under Rule 40 — questions to private members relate to Bills, Resolutions, or matters for which they bear legislative responsibility.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Statement 1 only is incorrect) tempts students who know about private member questions but wrongly accept Statement 2 as true, not realising backbenchers of the ruling party also have full question rights.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Rule 40 allows questions to private members on Bills and Resolutions they are responsible for — 'never to private members' is categorically false; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Question Hour is open to all members, including ruling party backbenchers — the claim of 'exclusive prerogative of Opposition' is false; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: A question about a private member's Bill directed at that private member is explicitly permitted — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect — select option (b): 1 and 2 only are NOT correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two independent misconceptions are tested simultaneously. The first — that only ministers can be questioned — ignores the rare but procedurally significant Rule 40 provision. The second — that Question Hour is an Opposition tool — is a political assumption with no procedural basis. Both are scope-extension errors where partial knowledge of parliamentary convention is overgeneralised into absolute rules.
solution.final_explanation:
Question Hour is a device available to all members of Parliament, not just Opposition MPs, and questions can — in specific circumstances — be directed at private members rather than ministers.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Under Lok Sabha Rule 40, a question may be addressed to a private member if it concerns a Bill, Resolution, or other matter for which that member bears responsibility. The absolute claim 'never' renders this statement false.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no procedural restriction that reserves Question Hour for Opposition members. Any member, including ruling party backbenchers, may ask questions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Questioning a private member on their own introduced Bill is the standard application of Rule 40 — this is procedurally valid.

Value Addition:
• Questions to private members are rare in practice but are a recognised procedural tool — a common MCQ trap.
• Ministers are questioned on matters within their ministerial portfolios — they cannot be questioned on purely personal matters.
• Question Hour is distinct from Private Members' Business, which relates to Bills and Resolutions introduced outside government time.

solution.concept_anchor: Supplementary questions — no advance notice required

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Supplementary questions can only arise after the oral answer to a Starred question and must stay within the scope of the original answer received.
statement_analysis.reason: Supplementaries are spawned by the oral answer to a Starred question; they cannot introduce new subject matter and are not permitted after Unstarred written answers.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: A member intending to ask a supplementary question must submit advance written notice to the Speaker at least 24 hours before the sitting.
statement_analysis.reason: Supplementary questions require no advance notice whatsoever — they are entirely spontaneous, arising from the minister's oral answer in real time. This is a defining characteristic that distinguishes them from the parent question.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect) is the correct answer and simultaneously serves as the intended answer; the strong distractor for students would be option (a) being confused with (c) — but here the format labels make (a) the correct answer since both statements' verdicts together map to option (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Supplementaries arise exclusively from Starred questions after their oral delivery; they cannot travel beyond the minister's answer — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: No prior notice is required for supplementary questions — the spontaneous, unscripted nature is precisely their defining feature; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect maps to option (c): Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 introduces a plausible-sounding procedural requirement — 24-hour advance notice — that mirrors the logic of the parent Starred question (which requires 15 days' notice). A student who applies the same logic to supplementaries will be misled. The critical understanding is that supplementaries are deliberately unscripted: requiring notice would defeat their entire purpose as a live accountability tool arising from the minister's actual words.
solution.final_explanation:
Supplementary questions are the live follow-up mechanism that gives Starred questions their particular accountability value — the ability to pursue an evasive or incomplete answer in real time.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Supplementaries are exclusively attached to Starred questions. After an oral answer, the questioning member (and sometimes other members, at the Speaker's discretion) may ask questions that arise directly from what was said. Introducing a fresh subject is not permitted.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No advance notice is required for supplementary questions. They are spontaneous by design — scripting them in advance would eliminate the element of genuine parliamentary scrutiny they are meant to provide.

Value Addition:
• There is no fixed numerical limit on supplementaries per question, but time constraints of Question Hour effectively limit them.
• The Speaker has full discretion to allow, disallow, or curtail supplementary questions.
• Supplementary questions are the primary reason Starred questions are considered more powerful accountability tools than Unstarred questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Admissibility conditions — sub-judice, arguments, Speaker's authority

statement_analysis.statement: A question containing ironical expressions or imputations is inadmissible during Question Hour.
statement_analysis.reason: The Rules of Procedure explicitly disallow questions that contain arguments, inferences, imputations, or ironical expressions — these compromise the neutral factual character required of parliamentary questions.

statement_analysis.statement: A matter pending before a court of law is automatically and unconditionally inadmissible as a question in Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The sub-judice restriction is not unconditional — the Speaker retains discretion to allow a question on a sub-judice matter if satisfied that its consideration will not prejudice the pending judicial proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker's decision on admissibility of a question can be appealed by the aggrieved member to a Committee of Privileges.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker is the sole and final authority on question admissibility — no appeal lies from this decision, including to any parliamentary committee.

statement_analysis.statement: A question must relate to a matter of public importance falling within the responsibility of the Government of India to be admissible.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a foundational admissibility criterion — questions on purely private matters or on subjects beyond the central government's jurisdiction are not admissible.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Only two) is the correct answer; students who believe sub-judice is an absolute bar will incorrectly count three correct statements and choose option (c).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Ironical expressions and imputations are explicitly listed as grounds for inadmissibility — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Speaker has discretion to allow sub-judice questions when judicial proceedings will not be prejudiced — 'automatic and unconditional' is false; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Speaker's admissibility decision is final; no appeal to Committee of Privileges or any other body — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 4: Public importance and governmental responsibility are the two core admissibility pillars — Statement 4 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 4 are correct — two correct items — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the primary trap: students who know the sub-judice rule exists will mark it as an absolute prohibition, missing the Speaker's discretionary exception. This converts a conditional rule into a falsely absolute one. Statement 3 traps students who conflate parliamentary privilege oversight (Committee of Privileges) with admissibility oversight — two entirely distinct domains.
solution.final_explanation:
Admissibility of questions is governed by a combination of procedural rules and the Speaker's discretionary authority. The rules are specific about what renders a question inadmissible, but they also preserve the Speaker's discretion in grey areas.

Consider the following statements regarding admissibility of questions in Parliament:

| Statement | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Contains ironical expressions or imputations — inadmissible | Correct |
| Sub-judice matter — automatic and unconditional bar | Incorrect |
| Speaker's admissibility decision appealable to Committee of Privileges | Incorrect |
| Must relate to public importance within GoI responsibility | Correct |

• Statement 1 — Correct: Arguments, inferences, imputations, and ironical expressions are explicitly prohibited by the Rules of Procedure.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Speaker retains discretion to permit questions on sub-judice matters when judicial proceedings will not be prejudiced — the bar is not absolute.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Speaker's decision on admissibility is final; no appeal mechanism exists.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Public importance and governmental jurisdiction are the foundational admissibility criteria.

Value Addition:
• Questions cannot anticipate a matter already listed on the Order Paper for the same sitting.
• The sub-judice restriction under Question Hour procedure is distinct from the sub-judice convention applying to parliamentary debates generally.
• A question on a State List subject is ordinarily inadmissible unless President's Rule is in force in that state.

solution.concept_anchor: Question Hour — Rules of Procedure basis, not constitutional mandate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a tempts students who correctly identify both A and R as true but assume that non-constitutional status of Question Hour is caused by Zero Hour's existence — a false causal link.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Question Hour derives from Rules of Procedure under Article 118, not from an express constitutional provision — A is factually correct.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Zero Hour does start at 12 noon and has no mention in the Constitution or Rules of Procedure — R is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Zero Hour's informal status is a separate fact about a different parliamentary device; it does not explain why Question Hour lacks direct constitutional mention. The two are independent procedural facts — R does NOT explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question places two true facts in an assertion-reason format where the temptation is to accept the causal link because both A and R are about the informal/non-statutory aspects of parliamentary devices. A student who reads superficially will see 'Question Hour not in Constitution' and 'Zero Hour not in rules' as a logical pair and choose (a). The correct analysis requires recognising that Zero Hour's status has absolutely no bearing on why Question Hour is rule-based rather than constitution-based — they are independent institutional facts.
solution.final_explanation:
Question Hour's procedural basis and Zero Hour's informal status are two frequently tested facts that are individually true but causally unconnected.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The Constitution does not expressly mandate Question Hour. Parliament's authority to regulate its own procedure flows from Article 118, under which the Rules of Procedure are framed. These Rules — not the Constitution itself — establish Question Hour, its timing, and its structure.
• Reason (R): Correct. Zero Hour begins at 12 noon and is entirely a parliamentary convention. It finds no mention in the Constitution or the Rules of Procedure — making it the most informally established feature of Indian parliamentary practice.
• Causal Link: R does not explain A. The reason Question Hour lacks direct constitutional mention has nothing to do with Zero Hour's existence or its own non-statutory character. These are independent facts about two separate parliamentary devices.

Value Addition:
• Article 118 is the constitutional source of Parliament's rule-making power for its own procedure.
• Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary innovation with no equivalent in the UK's Westminster Parliament.
• Question Hour's suspension (as in 2020 Monsoon Session due to COVID-19) requires only a decision under the Rules of Procedure — no constitutional amendment is needed.

solution.concept_anchor: Suspension of Question Hour — Rules of Procedure suffice, no amendment needed
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because a constitutional emergency context makes students instinctively look for a constitutional provision or Presidential order to suspend a parliamentary feature, when in fact the Rules of Procedure are self-sufficient.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): A resolution of the House is not required — the Speaker, exercising powers under the Rules of Procedure, can suspend Question Hour without a formal House resolution.
Eliminate (b): No Presidential Order or Proclamation is required to suspend Question Hour — this is a parliamentary procedural matter governed entirely by the Rules of Procedure.
Eliminate (c): A constitutional amendment is not needed — suspending Question Hour requires no change to the Constitution since Question Hour is itself rule-based, not constitutionally mandated.

Confirm (d): The Speaker can suspend or curtail Question Hour using existing powers under the Rules of Procedure — no additional legal instrument is required, as demonstrated during the 2020 Monsoon Session.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario involves a national emergency context, which triggers a student's instinct to reach for constitutional provisions or Presidential orders. Options (b) and (c) exploit this instinct by offering procedurally significant-sounding instruments. The correct understanding requires knowing that Question Hour is procedural, not constitutional — its suspension therefore operates within the procedural domain, requiring no higher authority than the Speaker acting under the Rules of Procedure.
solution.final_explanation:
When a national emergency is declared and Parliament is in session, certain adjustments to parliamentary proceedings may become necessary. The question is whether suspending Question Hour requires a special legal instrument beyond the existing Rules of Procedure.

The applicable principle: Question Hour is established by the Rules of Procedure under Article 118 — it has no independent constitutional status. Therefore, any modification or suspension of Question Hour falls entirely within the procedural domain. The Speaker, exercising authority under the Rules of Procedure, can suspend or curtail Question Hour without requiring a House resolution, a Presidential order, or a constitutional amendment.

• Option (a): Incorrect — a formal House resolution is not required; Speaker's authority under the Rules suffices.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Presidential orders or proclamations are irrelevant to internal parliamentary scheduling matters.
• Option (c): Incorrect — no constitutional amendment is possible or necessary for a procedural matter like this.
• Option (d): Correct — the Speaker can act under the existing Rules of Procedure; the 2020 COVID-19 precedent (Monsoon Session suspension of Question Hour) demonstrates this clearly.

Value Addition:
• During the 2020 Monsoon Session, Question Hour was suspended citing COVID-19 — this is the most cited real-world precedent.
• The Speaker can also curtail (shorten) rather than fully suspend Question Hour based on circumstances.
• Zero Hour was also suspended in the same 2020 session, reinforcing that both devices are procedural in nature.

concepts_used: Half-Hour Discussion: Arising Out of Question Hour

solution.concept_anchor: Half-Hour Discussion vs. Short Duration Discussion — distinct devices
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Short Duration Discussion) is the strong distractor because students who know it is Rule 193 may confuse it with a device that also 'arises from Question Hour,' when in fact only Half-Hour Discussion has that specific origin.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: which parliamentary devices arise directly from, or are triggered by, a matter already raised during Question Hour?
Half-Hour Discussion — explicitly arises from a question already answered in Question Hour or in writing; directly linked.
Supplementary questions — arise directly from the oral answer given during Question Hour; directly linked.
Starred questions — themselves constitute the core of Question Hour; directly linked.

Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193) — an independent device for raising urgent matters of public importance; does NOT require a prior Question Hour peg and is NOT triggered by Question Hour. This is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193) and Half-Hour Discussion are the most commonly conflated parliamentary devices. Both involve brief discussions without formal motions or voting. The critical difference is that Half-Hour Discussion must arise from a question already answered in Question Hour, while Short Duration Discussion is an independent device not tied to Question Hour. Students who know both devices exist but do not know their procedural triggers will confuse the two.
solution.final_explanation:
The category tested here is: parliamentary devices that are procedurally connected to or triggered by Question Hour.

• Option (a) — Starred questions: These are the core of Question Hour itself — they are directly within Question Hour. Not the odd one out.
• Option (b) — Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193): This is the odd one out. Rule 193 discussions are an independent parliamentary device for raising urgent matters — they do not require a Question Hour peg and are not triggered by anything that happened in Question Hour.
• Option (c) — Half-Hour Discussion: Specifically arises from a question already answered during Question Hour (or in writing) — it has a direct procedural link to Question Hour.
• Option (d) — Supplementary questions: These arise during Question Hour itself, triggered by the minister's oral answer to a Starred question.

Value Addition:
• Half-Hour Discussion is held during the last 30 minutes of the sitting on three days per week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday in Lok Sabha).
• Short Duration Discussion under Rule 193 allows members to raise urgent matters of public importance without a formal motion.
• Neither Half-Hour Discussion nor Short Duration Discussion involves formal voting — both are purely deliberative.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajya Sabha Chairman — presiding authority, not Speaker

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The presiding authority over Question Hour in the Rajya Sabha is the Chairman, who is the Vice President of India — not the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: The Vice President of India serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and presides over its proceedings, including Question Hour — distinct from the Lok Sabha Speaker.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, questions that have been admitted and placed on the Order Paper of the Rajya Sabha also lapse since Rajya Sabha's business is linked to the tenure of the Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body — it does not dissolve when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Rajya Sabha questions do not lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha; only Lok Sabha questions lapse.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) tempts students who know Statement 1 is correct and wrongly extend the lapsing principle to Rajya Sabha by analogy with Lok Sabha.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha and presides over Question Hour there — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Rajya Sabha is a permanent, continuing house — it does not dissolve with the Lok Sabha; its admitted questions do not lapse on Lok Sabha dissolution — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the lapsing principle by extending it incorrectly to the Rajya Sabha. Students who know that Lok Sabha questions lapse on dissolution may mechanically apply the same rule to Rajya Sabha without recalling the foundational difference — the Rajya Sabha is a continuing body and cannot be dissolved. This entity-swap error (applying a Lok Sabha rule to the Rajya Sabha) is a classic UPSC distractor mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
The Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha operate under distinct procedural regimes reflecting their different constitutional characters.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Vice President of India, as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, presides over all Rajya Sabha proceedings including Question Hour. Confusing the Chairman with the Speaker is the most basic — and most frequently tested — error in Rajya Sabha questions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Rajya Sabha is constitutionally described as a permanent body that cannot be dissolved. When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, only Lok Sabha's admitted questions (and pending Bills, with exceptions) lapse. Rajya Sabha's business, including admitted questions, continues unaffected.

Value Addition:
• The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides in the Chairman's absence — not the Speaker or Deputy Speaker.
• Bills pending in the Rajya Sabha do not lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha — this is a parallel distinction that is tested alongside lapsing of questions.
• The Rajya Sabha also follows a 15-day notice period for Starred and Unstarred questions, similar to the Lok Sabha.

solution.concept_anchor: Ballot system — Starred questions converted to Unstarred when not reached
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because students who know the ballot determines oral listing may assume all non-balloted questions are simply dropped, not realising they are converted to Unstarred status and answered in writing.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The ballot does not work on a first-come-first-served basis — it is a random ballot to ensure fairness among all submitted Starred questions.
Eliminate (c): Starred questions not selected in the ballot do not lapse — they are converted to Unstarred status and receive written answers.
Eliminate (d): Non-selected questions are not entirely omitted; they receive written answers as Unstarred questions — the member's question still gets a response.

Confirm (b): Only approximately 20 Starred questions are listed daily through the ballot; the remainder are automatically converted to Unstarred and answered in written form — option (b) correctly captures this two-stage process.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap operates on the assumption that 'Starred' means oral, making students assume non-selected Starred questions simply lapse or are dropped. The procedural reality is more nuanced — a member's Starred question submission is not wasted; it is downgraded to Unstarred and answered in writing. This blurs the Starred/Unstarred distinction in practice and is a high-yield UPSC examination point.
solution.final_explanation:
The ballot system manages the volume of Starred questions submitted daily in the Lok Sabha.

• Option (a): Incorrect — the listing of Starred questions for oral answers is determined by a random ballot, not by the order of submission (first-come-first-served).
• Option (b): Correct — only about 20 Starred questions are listed per day through the ballot. Starred questions not selected through the ballot are converted to Unstarred status and answered in written form, appended to the proceedings.
• Option (c): Incorrect — non-selected Starred questions do not lapse; they are converted and answered in writing. Lapsing of questions occurs when Lok Sabha itself is dissolved.
• Option (d): Incorrect — questions not reached through the ballot still receive written answers; they are not omitted from the records.

Value Addition:
• Lok Sabha Rule 33 governs the ballot system for Starred questions.
• A member may submit up to one Starred question per day — the ballot system therefore applies across all members' submissions.
• In practice, the conversion of Starred to Unstarred status means even 'oral' questions frequently end up as written answers — a limitation on Question Hour's real-time accountability function.

concepts_used: Parliamentary Privilege and Question Hour: Immunity of Questions and Answers

solution.concept_anchor: Article 105(1) — absolute privilege for speech in Parliament

statement_analysis.statement: A member of Parliament enjoys absolute privilege under Article 105(1) for any question asked or statement made during Question Hour and cannot be sued in any court for defamation.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 105(1) grants members absolute immunity for anything said or done in the exercise of their powers as members — this covers questions and statements during Question Hour without exception.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary privilege under Article 105(1) also protects a member from any action that the House itself may take for a breach of privilege arising from their conduct during Question Hour.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 105(1) protects members from external legal proceedings (courts, civil suits) but does NOT protect them from the House's own disciplinary powers — the House can take action for breach of privilege even for conduct during parliamentary proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: A minister who deliberately provides misleading information in response to a question during Question Hour can be held accountable through a breach of privilege motion.
statement_analysis.reason: Deliberately misleading the House is considered a contempt of Parliament — a breach of privilege motion can be brought against a minister for providing false or misleading answers during Question Hour, notwithstanding the general privilege protection.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 and wrongly assume privilege also protects against the House's own disciplinary action.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 105(1) provides absolute protection from court proceedings for speech in Parliament — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Privilege protects from external suits; the House retains power to discipline its own members — 'also protects from the House itself' is false; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Deliberate misleading of the House is a recognised ground for breach of privilege proceedings — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → select option (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a common over-extension of the privilege concept. Students who correctly understand that privilege protects members from civil and criminal liability outside Parliament often assume this immunity extends to the House's own disciplinary mechanisms. This is the critical scope-extension error — privilege immunises members from external authority, not from the House's inherent power to regulate its own members.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary privilege under Article 105 is a nuanced protection — absolute in some directions, irrelevant in others.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 105(1) grants members complete freedom of speech in Parliament and immunity from court proceedings. Anything said during Question Hour — including pointed questions or critical statements — is protected from defamation suits or criminal proceedings.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Privilege shields members from external legal action but emphatically does not shield them from the House's own disciplinary authority. A member can face a breach of privilege motion, suspension, or reprimand by the House for conduct during proceedings.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Deliberately misleading the House through a Question Hour answer constitutes contempt of Parliament. A breach of privilege motion is the procedural vehicle for holding a minister accountable in such circumstances.

Value Addition:
• Article 105(2) extends privilege to committees and their proceedings.
• Privilege protects publication of parliamentary debates only when it is official — extracts published privately may not enjoy full protection.
• The scope of parliamentary privilege is not defined exhaustively in the Constitution — it continues to evolve through parliamentary practice and judicial interpretation.

solution.concept_anchor: President's Rule — makes state administration questions admissible in Parliament
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d tempts students who know the Reason about Article 356 is correct but wrongly conclude the Assertion is incorrect because they believe Parliament can never ask about State subjects.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? During President's Rule under Article 356, Parliament legislates for the state and the state administration falls under central government responsibility — questions about that state's administration become admissible in Parliament. A is factually correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Article 356 and Schedule VII together do create the constitutional basis for Parliament assuming legislative and administrative authority over a state under President's Rule — R is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes — the reason questions on a state's administration become admissible during President's Rule is precisely because Article 356 shifts legislative responsibility for that state to Parliament; central ministers then become accountable for that state's administration. R correctly explains the mechanism behind A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap targets students who know that State List questions are ordinarily inadmissible and overapply this rule even to the President's Rule exception. Such students will mark A as incorrect (leading them to option d) without recognising that the assertion is carefully qualified with 'during President's Rule.' The Reason accurately identifies the constitutional mechanism (Article 356) that creates this exception — making this a genuine case where both A and R are correct and causally linked.
solution.final_explanation:
Questions on State List subjects are ordinarily inadmissible in Parliament because central ministers bear no responsibility for state subjects. President's Rule creates a critical exception to this principle.

• Assertion (A): Correct. When President's Rule is proclaimed under Article 356, Parliament assumes the legislative authority of the state legislature and the central government takes over the state's executive functions. Central ministers become responsible for the state's administration — making questions about that state's affairs admissible during Question Hour.
• Reason (R): Correct. Article 356 enables the proclamation of President's Rule; Schedule VII defines the three-list distribution of legislative powers. Together, they create the constitutional framework under which Parliament's legislative competence is expanded to cover state subjects during the period of President's Rule.
• Causal Link: R directly explains A — the admissibility of questions on a state's administration during President's Rule flows from the constitutional shift of responsibility effected by Article 356.

Value Addition:
• President's Rule can be proclaimed for six months and extended up to three years with periodic parliamentary approval.
• A Central law that covers a State List subject is another ground for admissibility of related questions in Parliament.
• The admissibility exception during President's Rule is a nuanced intersection of Question Hour procedure and constitutional emergency provisions — a high-value cross-concept area.

solution.concept_anchor: Westminster vs. Indian Parliament — key procedural differences
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps the placement of Zero Hour (Indian innovation) with PMQs (Westminster feature), exploiting the surface similarity between both being 'special question formats.'
elimination_logic: Match A (Prime Minister's Questions / PMQs): This is a dedicated weekly session in the UK Parliament where the PM faces questions — India has no equivalent PMQ session. Matches with 3.
Match B (Zero Hour): Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary innovation not found in Westminster — explicitly noted as India's original contribution to parliamentary practice. Matches with 1.

Match C (Starred questions — oral with supplementaries): This is a feature of the Indian Parliament's structured Starred/Unstarred classification; UK Parliament has different conventions for oral questions. Matches with 4.

Match D (Unstarred questions — written answers only): The written answer format for Unstarred questions is a formal classification used in the Indian Parliament. Matches with 2. Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the concept of 'special question formats' — Zero Hour and PMQs are both departures from ordinary Question Hour, making students associate them as equivalent devices. The critical difference is that PMQs is a structured, formal, rule-based weekly session in Westminster while Zero Hour is an informal convention unique to India. Matching them incorrectly (B-3, A-1) is the most common error this question is designed to catch.
solution.final_explanation:
Indian Parliament borrowed the Question Hour structure from Westminster but made significant adaptations and innovations.

Correct matches:
• A–3: Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs) is a weekly feature of the UK Parliament where the Prime Minister faces questions from members — India has no equivalent dedicated PMQ session. The Indian PM can be questioned during ordinary Question Hour but there is no reserved PMQ slot.
• B–1: Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary innovation — it has no parallel in the Westminster Parliament and represents India's original contribution to parliamentary convention.
• C–4: The Starred question format (oral answer with supplementaries permitted) is part of India's structured classification — UK oral questions operate under different procedural conventions.
• D–2: Unstarred questions receiving only written answers constitute the formal written-answer mechanism in the Indian Parliament.

Value Addition:
• India's Zero Hour is frequently cited as evidence of Indian parliamentary originality beyond the Westminster template.
• The UK does not use the Starred/Unstarred classification — oral and written questions operate under separate but differently structured conventions.
• Indian Parliament also differs from Westminster in having a constitutionally codified privilege framework (Article 105) rather than relying entirely on common law privilege.

concepts_used: Lapsing of Questions: When a Lok Sabha is Dissolved

solution.concept_anchor: Lapsing sequence — admission, Order Paper placement, dissolution effect
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b places dissolution before Order Paper listing, tempting students who believe questions lapse only at the admission stage, not after being listed.
elimination_logic: Establish Step 1: A member submits the question — this is the earliest action in the sequence.
Establish Step 2: The Speaker's Secretariat examines and admits the question — admission follows submission.
Establish Step 3: The admitted question is listed on the Order Paper for a specific sitting — this happens after admission.

Establish Step 4: Lok Sabha is dissolved before the sitting arrives — dissolution causes lapse even at this final stage. The UPSC trap is that lapsing occurs even after Order Paper listing, not just at earlier stages.
Correct sequence: Submission → Admission → Order Paper listing → Dissolution (and lapse) → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap tests whether students know that questions lapse on dissolution regardless of how advanced their processing stage is. Many students believe questions lapse only if not yet admitted — the UPSC-tested point is that even questions that have been admitted AND listed on the Order Paper lapse if the Lok Sabha is dissolved before that sitting takes place. The chronology format forces precision about which stage precedes which.
solution.final_explanation:
The life cycle of a parliamentary question in the Lok Sabha involves distinct procedural stages, and dissolution terminates the process at any point.

Correct chronological sequence:
1. Submission: Member files the question within the permitted daily limit.
2. Admission: Speaker's Secretariat examines the question for admissibility (public importance, not sub-judice, no imputations, etc.) and formally admits it.
3. Order Paper listing: The admitted question is listed on the Order Paper for a specific future sitting, potentially through the ballot for Starred questions.
4. Dissolution with lapse: If Lok Sabha is dissolved before the sitting date arrives, the question lapses — even though it has been admitted and listed.

The critical UPSC point is that lapsing occurs at dissolution regardless of stage — even an Order Paper-listed question is not immune. Option (d) correctly places dissolution last in the sequence, after all processing is complete.

Value Addition:
• Rajya Sabha questions do not lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha — the Rajya Sabha is a permanent body.
• Bills also lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha, with exceptions (e.g., Bills pending in Rajya Sabha do not lapse).
• Questions lapse on prorogation only if the session ends before they are reached — prorogation (unlike dissolution) does not permanently kill a question.

Admissibility Conditions for Questions

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker's finality on admissibility — no appeal

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker can disallow a question that relates to a matter exclusively within the State List unless the Union Government has a specific interest in the subject.
statement_analysis.reason: The rule is not about 'Union Government having a specific interest' — the admissibility criterion is that the matter must be within the responsibility of the Government of India. State List subjects are inadmissible unless specific conditions (like President's Rule or a Central law) apply; 'specific interest' is a vague and non-existent procedural standard.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker's decision on admissibility of a question is final and cannot be challenged in any court or appealed within the House.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker is the sole and final authority on question admissibility — no internal appeal mechanism exists, and courts do not interfere with the internal proceedings of Parliament under Article 212.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker can allow a Short Notice Question at their discretion even when the Minister has indicated unwillingness to answer it.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Speaker decides admissibility of a Short Notice Question, a Minister retains the right to decline to answer if not prepared — the Speaker's admission does not override the Minister's procedural right to decline. The Speaker can admit; they cannot compel the answer.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Statement 1 only is incorrect) tempts students who correctly identify Statement 1's flaw but wrongly accept Statement 3 as valid, not knowing that ministerial refusal to answer a Short Notice Question is procedurally protected.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 'Specific interest' is not a recognised admissibility standard — the correct criterion is governmental responsibility; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Speaker's finality on admissibility is well-established — no appeal exists internally or judicially; Statement 2 is correct, so it is NOT the answer to 'which is NOT correct.'

Evaluate Statement 3: The Speaker admitting a Short Notice Question does not remove the Minister's right to decline answering — the claim that the Speaker can effectively compel the answer by admitting the question is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are both NOT correct → select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the subtle trap: it sounds like a natural extension of the Speaker's admitted power — 'if the Speaker admits, surely the Minister must answer.' This plausible-fabrication exploits the assumption that admissibility and compelled response are linked. They are not — admissibility is the Speaker's domain; the Minister's willingness to answer is a separate procedural prerogative. A student who conflates these two distinct powers will incorrectly mark Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker's powers over Question Hour are substantial but have clear boundaries — admissibility and compelled response are distinct.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The admissibility standard is whether the matter falls within the responsibility of the Government of India — not whether the Union has a 'specific interest.' This fabricated standard does not exist in the Rules of Procedure.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Speaker's admissibility decision is final. Article 212 bars courts from inquiring into parliamentary proceedings, and no internal appeal mechanism exists against the Speaker's ruling on admissibility.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: A Minister may decline to answer a Short Notice Question citing unpreparedness. The Speaker's decision to admit the question only clears the procedural hurdle of admissibility — it does not compel the Minister to provide an answer.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker can disallow questions that are repetitive, sub-judice, or seek information already publicly available.
• Questions relating to State List subjects become admissible during President's Rule — this is the principal exception to the 'governmental responsibility' criterion.
• The Speaker's authority over supplementary questions is equally final — they can disallow supplementaries that introduce new subject matter.

solution.concept_anchor: Half-Hour Discussion — deliberative, no voting, three days per week
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because it correctly identifies the three-day schedule but incorrectly adds voting, which is not a feature of Half-Hour Discussion.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Half-Hour Discussion is deliberative — no formal motion is moved and no voting takes place; it is held on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday in Lok Sabha during the last 30 minutes — this pair is correctly matched.
Evaluate (b): 'Any day of the week' is incorrect — Half-Hour Discussion is scheduled for three specific days per week, not any day; this pair is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate (c): A formal vote does NOT take place in Half-Hour Discussion — despite the correct days mentioned, the voting claim makes this pair incorrect.
Evaluate (d): Half-Hour Discussion arises from a question already answered, not from matters introduced independently without any prior Question Hour peg — this pair is incorrectly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges features of Half-Hour Discussion with Short Duration Discussion. Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193) can be raised independently; Half-Hour Discussion requires a Question Hour peg. Additionally, option (c) correctly names three days of the week (a strong memory marker) but adds voting — a feature that does not exist in Half-Hour Discussion. Students who associate 'three days a week' with the correct option may not carefully check the voting claim.
solution.final_explanation:
Half-Hour Discussion is a specific, time-bound, deliberative device tied directly to Question Hour.

• Option (a): Correctly matched — Half-Hour Discussion is a deliberative device with no formal motion or voting. It is scheduled on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday (three days per week) in Lok Sabha, held during the last 30 minutes of the sitting.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched — 'any day of the week' is wrong; the three-day schedule is fixed.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched — voting does not occur in Half-Hour Discussion despite the correct identification of three days.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — Half-Hour Discussion must arise from a question already answered in Question Hour or in writing; it cannot be initiated independently.

Value Addition:
• A minister may make a brief statement during Half-Hour Discussion but is not obliged to do so — no vote of confidence or censure follows.
• Half-Hour Discussion is distinct from Adjournment Motion, which requires a definite, urgent matter of recent public importance and can lead to a vote.
• The procedural basis for Half-Hour Discussion is separate from Rule 193, which governs Short Duration Discussions.

solution.concept_anchor: Starred vs. Unstarred — limits, ballot, conversion mechanism

statement_analysis.statement: A member of the Lok Sabha may submit up to one Starred question and up to ten Unstarred questions per day.
statement_analysis.reason: The Rules of Procedure prescribe a daily limit of one Starred question and up to ten Unstarred questions per member — reflecting the more demanding oral-answer format of Starred questions.

statement_analysis.statement: All Starred questions submitted by members for a given day are listed on the Order Paper for oral answers.
statement_analysis.reason: Only approximately 20 Starred questions are listed for oral answers per day, selected through a ballot. The rest are converted to Unstarred status and answered in writing — not all submitted Starred questions reach the oral stage.

statement_analysis.statement: A Starred question that is not reached during Question Hour due to time constraints is automatically converted to an Unstarred question and answered in writing.
statement_analysis.reason: Questions listed for oral answers but not reached within the one-hour Question Hour are treated as Unstarred and their answers are appended to the proceedings in written form.

statement_analysis.statement: Supplementary questions asked during Question Hour are also subject to the daily numerical limit prescribed for Starred questions.
statement_analysis.reason: Supplementary questions are spontaneous follow-ups and have no prescribed numerical limit — they are governed only by the Speaker's discretion and the available time, not by any pre-set quota.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) tempts students who accept Statement 3 but are uncertain about Statement 4, leading them to count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: One Starred and ten Unstarred per day per member — correctly stated; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Not all Starred questions are listed — only ~20 through ballot; the rest convert to Unstarred; 'All... listed for oral answers' is false; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Unstarred conversion of un-reached Starred questions is standard practice; Statement 3 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Supplementaries have no numerical daily limit — they are subject only to time and Speaker's discretion; Statement 4 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — two correct → select option (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the primary trap — a student who knows supplementaries have 'no fixed limit' may still incorrectly reason that the ballot-based daily ceiling for Starred questions logically extends to supplementaries. This partial-truth error assumes consistent application of a rule across related but distinct procedural categories. Supplementaries and Starred questions are governed by entirely different procedural logics.
solution.final_explanation:
The daily question limits and the ballot-conversion mechanism are two of the most precisely tested procedural details of Question Hour.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 1 starred + 10 unstarred daily per member | Correct |
| All Starred questions listed for oral answers | Incorrect |
| Un-reached Starred questions convert to Unstarred | Correct |
| Supplementaries subject to numerical daily limit | Incorrect |

• Statement 1 — Correct: The one Starred / ten Unstarred daily limit is a key procedural fact.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The ballot determines which ~20 Starred questions are listed; the rest convert to Unstarred — all submissions do not reach oral stage.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The conversion of un-reached Starred questions to Unstarred is how the House ensures all submitted questions receive some form of response.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Supplementaries are entirely spontaneous — no pre-set limit applies; only the Speaker's control and time constraints govern them.

Value Addition:
• Lok Sabha Rule 33 governs the ballot for Starred questions.
• The conversion mechanism (Starred to Unstarred) is the practical reason why the distinction between the two categories is less sharp in daily practice than in theory.
• A member may submit fewer than the maximum daily limit — the limit is a ceiling, not a floor.

solution.concept_anchor: Zero Hour — Indian innovation, no constitutional or rule-based status
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who associate Zero Hour with urgency and public importance may assume it must have some statutory backing in the Parliamentary Proceedings Act (a plausible-sounding but non-existent statute for this purpose).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Zero Hour is not a constitutional provision — the Constitution does not mention it; eliminating this confirms its informal nature.
Eliminate (b): No Parliamentary Proceedings Act establishes Zero Hour — this is a plausible-fabrication distractor; Zero Hour has no statutory basis.
Eliminate (d): Zero Hour is not a convention borrowed from Westminster — it is an Indian parliamentary innovation; the British Parliament has no equivalent device.
Confirm (c): Zero Hour starts at 12 noon, has no mention in the Constitution or the Rules of Procedure, and is purely an Indian parliamentary convention — option (c) correctly describes its status.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) introduces a fictitious 'Parliamentary Proceedings Act' — a plausible-fabrication that sounds authoritative to a student who knows that many parliamentary features have statutory or rule-based foundations. The distinction being tested is that Zero Hour is uniquely non-statutory and non-constitutional — a 'pure convention' that stands alone among Indian parliamentary devices in having absolutely no written rule-base.
solution.final_explanation:
Zero Hour is the most informally established device in Indian parliamentary practice.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Zero Hour has no constitutional provision; the Constitution does not mention it at all.
• Option (b): Incorrect — no Parliamentary Proceedings Act establishes or governs Zero Hour; this is a fabricated authority.
• Option (c): Correct — Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary convention that begins at 12 noon, immediately after Question Hour. It has no mention in the Constitution, the Rules of Procedure, or any statute. Members raise urgent matters of public importance on their own initiative, and the government is not obligated to respond.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Zero Hour is specifically an Indian parliamentary innovation; the British Westminster Parliament has no equivalent convention.

Value Addition:
• Zero Hour's informal status means it can be suspended without any procedural formality — as occurred during the 2020 Monsoon Session.
• During Zero Hour, members do not need to give advance notice, unlike Question Hour's 15-day minimum.
• Zero Hour demonstrates that parliamentary practice can develop powerful accountability conventions outside formal rule-making.

solution.concept_anchor: Question Hour effectiveness — disruptions, COVID-19 precedent, reform proposals

statement_analysis.statement: Frequent disruptions and adjournments of the House result in Question Hour being curtailed or lost, thereby weakening the daily executive accountability function it is designed to perform.
statement_analysis.reason: Question Hour is the first hour of business — when the House is adjourned due to disruptions at the start of a sitting, Question Hour is disproportionately affected, reducing the volume of ministerial accountability exercised through this device.

statement_analysis.statement: The suspension of Question Hour during the 2020 Monsoon Session of Parliament was authorised by a Presidential Proclamation citing the COVID-19 public health emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2020 Monsoon Session suspension of Question Hour was decided under the Rules of Procedure — no Presidential Proclamation was involved. Question Hour's procedural (non-constitutional) basis means its suspension requires only a procedural decision, not a constitutional instrument.

statement_analysis.statement: One reform proposal to strengthen parliamentary accountability is the creation of a dedicated Question Time for the Prime Minister, similar to the Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs) in the United Kingdom.
statement_analysis.reason: Establishing a PMQ-equivalent session in India is a frequently discussed reform, inspired by the UK practice where the PM faces structured questioning — India currently has no dedicated PM question session within Question Hour.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1 and 3 only) is the correct answer; students who mistakenly accept Statement 2 (due to the COVID precedent being real, even if the mechanism described is wrong) will choose option (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Disruptions disproportionately affect Question Hour as the first hour — this is a recognised accountability concern backed by PRS Legislative Research data; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The 2020 suspension was effected under the Rules of Procedure, not a Presidential Proclamation — introducing a Presidential Proclamation is a procedural fabrication; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: A dedicated PM question session is a known reform proposal in Indian parliamentary discourse; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is carefully calibrated: the COVID-19 Monsoon Session suspension is a well-known fact, making students assume the statement is correct. The trap is in the mechanism — 'Presidential Proclamation' is a constitutional instrument used for emergencies, not for internal parliamentary scheduling. A student with partial knowledge (knows the 2020 suspension happened) will mark Statement 2 as correct without scrutinising the mechanism described.
solution.final_explanation:
Question Hour's accountability function has come under increasing scholarly and parliamentary scrutiny in recent years.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Since Question Hour is the first hour of each sitting, any disruption that forces an adjournment at the start of the day eliminates Question Hour entirely. PRS Legislative Research has documented the significant number of Question Hour hours lost to disruptions over successive Lok Sabhas.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 2020 Monsoon Session suspension of Question Hour was decided through the Rules of Procedure — a purely procedural instrument. No Presidential Proclamation was issued or required. This is the key procedural distinction: Question Hour's non-constitutional basis means its suspension operates entirely within the procedural domain.
• Statement 3 — Correct: A dedicated PMQ-style session for the Indian Prime Minister is among the most discussed parliamentary reforms. Currently, the PM can be questioned during ordinary Question Hour but holds no dedicated question slot.

Value Addition:
• PRS Legislative Research tracks parliament's productive hours — a useful data source for UPSC GS Paper 2 governance questions.
• The UK PMQ session occurs weekly (Wednesdays) for 30 minutes — a structured, high-profile accountability event.
• Strengthening parliamentary committees is another suggested complement to Question Hour's declining effectiveness.

solution.concept_anchor: Sub-judice restriction — procedural rule, not constitutional prohibition

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The restriction on questions relating to sub-judice matters during Question Hour is a limitation imposed by the Rules of Procedure, not a prohibition mandated by the Constitution itself.
statement_analysis.reason: The sub-judice rule in Question Hour derives from the Rules of Procedure and the Speaker's practice — it is procedural, not a constitutionally mandated prohibition. This is a tested conceptual distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The sub-judice restriction applicable to questions in Question Hour and the restriction on parliamentary debates regarding pending court cases both operate on identical constitutional grounds under Article 105.
statement_analysis.reason: While Article 105 deals with parliamentary privilege, the sub-judice convention in debates operates on convention and comity grounds, and the Question Hour sub-judice rule operates under the Rules of Procedure — they are based on different grounds, not identical constitutional foundations.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) tempts students who broadly know that Article 105 governs parliamentary speech protections and assume all speech-related restrictions originate from the same constitutional provision.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Sub-judice restriction on questions is a Rule of Procedure limitation — it has no direct constitutional mandate; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The sub-judice convention for debates and the Question Hour rule on sub-judice operate on different grounds — comity and convention for debates, Rules of Procedure for questions — they are not on 'identical constitutional grounds'; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the plausible assumption that since both relate to sub-judice matters in parliamentary settings, they must share the same constitutional basis. This scope-extension error generalises from the true fact (Article 105 governs privilege) to the false conclusion (all sub-judice restrictions have identical constitutional grounding). The two restrictions — Question Hour Rule and the debate convention — have different procedural roots.
solution.final_explanation:
Sub-judice restrictions appear in two distinct parliamentary contexts, and their legal grounding differs importantly.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The rule against questions on sub-judice matters during Question Hour is found in the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business. It is not a constitutional prohibition — the Constitution does not itself bar questions on pending court cases. The Speaker retains discretion to allow such questions when satisfied they will not prejudice judicial proceedings.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The sub-judice convention in parliamentary debates (restraining members from discussing pending cases) operates on the basis of comity with the judiciary and parliamentary convention — not on Article 105 grounds. The Question Hour sub-judice rule operates under the Rules of Procedure. These are distinct bases, not identical constitutional grounds.

Value Addition:
• Article 105(1) protects members' freedom of speech in Parliament — it grants immunity but does not define the rules governing admissibility of questions.
• The Speaker's discretionary power to allow sub-judice questions when judicial prejudice is unlikely is a rarely used but procedurally significant power.
• The sub-judice restriction for debates is itself a matter of convention rather than strict legal rule — a member who raises a sub-judice matter in debate may face the Chair's intervention but not a court sanction.

solution.concept_anchor: Rule 40 — questions to private members on their Bills
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because students who know that bills are the subject of Private Members' Business may assume this scenario must be resolved during Private Members' Business time, not Question Hour.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable rule: The scenario involves a question directed at a non-minister MP regarding a Bill that member has introduced — this is precisely the scenario envisaged under Lok Sabha Rule 40.
Eliminate (a): Disqualification is not relevant — there is no bar on submitting such a question; the member has simply exercised a valid procedural right.
Eliminate (c): This scenario need not wait for Private Members' Business time — Rule 40 allows the question to be raised during Question Hour itself.
Eliminate (d): The Speaker does not automatically refer such questions to the Public Accounts Committee — this is a fabricated procedural step with no basis in Rule 40.

Confirm (b): Under Rule 40, the Speaker may admit the question and list it for oral answer during Question Hour — the non-minister MP must be given an opportunity to respond. Option (b) correctly identifies the applicable procedural principle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here replaces the minister (the usual recipient of questions) with a private member, disorienting students who associate Question Hour exclusively with ministerial accountability. Option (d) further confuses by suggesting a committee referral — a procedural step that might apply in other parliamentary contexts but has no basis in Rule 40. Students who know Rule 40 exists but are uncertain of its mechanics will gravitate toward option (d) as a procedurally plausible-sounding alternative.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario tests the little-known but procedurally significant provision under Lok Sabha Rule 40, which allows questions to be addressed to private members (non-ministers) under specific conditions.

The applicable principle: Under Rule 40, a question may be addressed to a private member if the subject matter relates to a Bill, Resolution, or other business for which that member bears responsibility. The Speaker decides admissibility and may list the question for oral answer during Question Hour — the private member then responds as if in a ministerial position for that limited purpose.

• Option (a): Incorrect — submitting such a question is not a procedural impropriety; Rule 40 expressly permits it.
• Option (b): Correct — the Speaker may admit the question and list it for Question Hour; the private member MP is obliged to respond on the matter of their Bill.
• Option (c): Incorrect — the question need not wait for Private Members' Business time; Rule 40 operates within Question Hour.
• Option (d): Incorrect — automatic referral to the Public Accounts Committee is not part of the Rule 40 procedure; this is a fabricated step.

Value Addition:
• Questions to private members are rare but constitute a recognised exception to the general rule that questions are addressed to ministers.
• Rule 40 is one of the least examined provisions of Lok Sabha procedure in practice but is frequently tested in UPSC questions.
• The Speaker's admissibility decision for private member questions follows the same general criteria as for ministerial questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Notice period hierarchy — 15 days standard, Short Notice exception
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c places Short Notice Question before standard notice, tempting students who associate urgency with the earliest stage of parliamentary procedure rather than an exception to it.
elimination_logic: Establish the standard sequence: The ordinary notice period of 15 days is the default starting point — members planning ordinary Starred or Unstarred questions must submit within this framework.
Short Notice Questions arise when urgency makes the 15-day period impractical — they are exceptions, not the starting point.
Matter reaching the floor for oral answer is the final stage — this happens during the actual Question Hour sitting, after notice, admission, and listing.

Correct sequence: Member submits question with standard 15-day notice → Speaker's Secretariat examines admissibility → If urgency arises, Short Notice route bypasses the 15-day requirement → Question is answered orally on the floor. Order: Standard notice framework (earliest reference point) → Admissibility examination → Short Notice as exception → Oral answer on floor → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap misorders the exception (Short Notice) and the rule (standard 15-day notice). Students who think of Short Notice Questions as the 'first' or 'default' procedure because they associate them with urgency and speed will reverse the logical sequence. The correct understanding is that the 15-day framework is the starting point; Short Notice is a deviation from it, available only when urgency justifies bypassing the standard period.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural sequence for questions in Lok Sabha follows a notice-admission-listing-answer logic, with Short Notice as a sanctioned exception at the notice stage.

Correct chronological sequence:
1. Standard 15-day notice framework: The Rules of Procedure set 15 days as the minimum notice for Starred and Unstarred questions — this is the default framework all members begin with.
2. Admissibility examination: The Speaker's Secretariat examines whether the question meets admissibility conditions.
3. Short Notice Question exception: When a matter is sufficiently urgent to justify bypassing the 15-day minimum, the Short Notice route allows the Speaker to admit the question with less notice — this is an exception that only becomes relevant after the standard framework is the reference point.
4. Oral answer on the floor: The admitted question is answered orally during Question Hour.

Option (a) correctly places the standard notice framework first, admissibility second, Short Notice exception third, and oral answer last.

Value Addition:
• A Minister may decline to answer even a Speaker-admitted Short Notice Question — urgency does not compel response.
• The 15-day notice period is set by the Rules of Procedure, not by the Constitution.
• Short Notice Questions, when answered, are answered orally — making them procedurally similar to Starred questions in their answer format.
